title: Rogue Wave Statistics from a Sparse Coherent Structure Decomposition
authors: Yuchen He, Amin Chabchoub, Zhan Wang
abstract: While conventional rogue wave statistical models rely on linear or weakly nonlinear descriptions of random seas, we demonstrate experimentally that moderately or strongly nonlinear wave fields can be represented by sparse ensembles of coherent soliton-like packets. These packets exhibit log-normal amplitude distributions together with uniformly distributed phases and peak emergence times. This sparse coherent structure framework naturally leads to an extreme value description in which the probability of exceedance is governed by the tail of the coherent-structure amplitude distribution. The prediction is validated against laboratory hydrodynamic experiments across a variety of unidirectional sea states, showing good agreement with the experimental observations and comparing favourably with conventional statistical prediction models while retaining analytical simplicity. Our results provide a direct physics-based link between sparse coherent structures and rogue wave probabilities, with broader implications for nonlinear wave physics in optics, cold gases, and plasmas.
summary: This paper introduces a novel framework to predict rogue wave statistics by decomposing the measured wave field into a sparse ensemble of localized, soliton-like packets. By analyzing the log-normal distribution of these extracted structures, the authors derive an extreme value theory that successfully predicts the heavy tails in wave exceedance probabilities, validating their approach against laboratory hydrodynamic experiments.
main_problem: Accurately predicting rogue wave statistics, which are extreme events in strongly nonlinear random wave fields.
main_result: The framework successfully predicts the heavy-tailed probability of exceedance for rogue waves by modeling the field as a sparse superposition of coherent soliton-like packets. This prediction shows good agreement with laboratory hydrodynamic experiments.
method: An iterative matching pursuit algorithm is used to decompose the complex wave envelope into a sparse ensemble of localized solitons, whose statistical properties (log-normal amplitude distribution) are then fed into an Extreme Value Theory framework.
model_or_system: The study analyzes rogue waves in deep-water random wave fields, using laboratory hydrodynamic experiments conducted in a wave flume. The underlying model treats the complex wave envelope as a sparse superposition of coherent soliton packets.
key_observables: Exceedance probability $P(> H)$, soliton amplitudes ($a$), number ($N$), and phase ($\phi$).
important_parameters: Sea state parameters like steepness ($\epsilon$) and peakedness ($\gamma$); the statistical moments ($\mu, \sigma$) derived from the extracted solitons.
main_assumptions: The complex wave envelope can be accurately represented as a sparse superposition of localized soliton-like packets; the iterative decomposition process yields a physically robust representation despite inherent non-uniqueness.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the successful reconstruction of the original wave envelope and phase using the extracted solitons, show the uniform distribution of soliton emergence times in 3D parameter space, and compare the predicted heavy-tailed exceedance probabilities against experimental data for various sea states.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitation of conventional statistical models. It then details the novel decomposition method (matching pursuit) to extract sparse solitons from measured wave fields. Finally, it applies Extreme Value Theory using the statistics of these extracted solitons to predict and validate rogue wave probabilities against experimental data across multiple sea states.
why_interesting: The methodology—using signal processing techniques like matching pursuit to decompose a complex random field into fundamental coherent structures whose statistical properties govern extreme events—is highly relevant for understanding nonlinear dynamics in optics or plasma physics where such decomposition methods are applicable.
